content.overview: BNS s. 53 — Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor. BNS restatement of IPC 113. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 113. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 53 is the rule on “Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor”. The section provides that when an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 53 exists so that “Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
53. When an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect

Essential ingredients
1. When an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z. B, in consequence of the instigation, causes grievous hurt to Z. Z dies in consequence. Here, if A knew that the grievous hurt abetted was likely to cause death, A is liable to be punished with the punishment provided for murder

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 53 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

learningObjectives: Understand the doctrine of unintended different effects under BNS s. 53.
Analyze the knowledge requirement: abettor must know the act was likely to cause that effect.
Distinguish between a different ACT (s. 51) and a different EFFECT of the same act (s. 53).
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 53 provides that when an act is abetted with the intention on the part of the abettor of causing a particular effect, and an act for which the abettor is liable in consequence of the abetment, causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor, the abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Where the physical act abetted causes a more severe or different physical consequence than the abettor specifically intended, the abettor is held liable for that graver consequence, provided he knew that the act was likely to produce that effect.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 53 (corresponding to IPC s. 113).
Scenario: The ACT abetted is done, but the EFFECT produced differs from that intended.
Threshold condition: Abettor must have known that the act abetted was 'likely to cause that effect'.
Liability: Punished as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that specific effect.
essentialIngredients: The abettor abetted an act intending a particular effect (e.g. grievous hurt).
The act caused a different or graver effect (e.g. death).
The abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that different effect.
The abettor is liable for the effect caused as if intended.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 53 deals with escalating RESULTS of the very act abetted. The distinction between s. 51 and s. 53 is vital: under s. 51, a DIFFERENT ACT is committed (e.g. abetted theft, perpetrator commits murder). Under s. 53, the VERY ACT abetted is committed (e.g. violent assault with iron rods), but it produces a DIFFERENT EFFECT (the victim dies instead of merely being injured). If A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z by smashing his chest with heavy stones, knowing that such trauma is likely to cause death, and Z dies, A is liable for murder/culpable homicide under s. 53.
examples: Teaching example (Grievous hurt causing death): A instigates B to cause grievous hurt to Z with an iron rod. A knows that the blows are likely to cause death. B strikes Z, and Z dies from the injuries. Under s. 53, A is liable for the murder of Z.

Teaching example (Unforeseeable death): A instigates B to give Z a simple slap on the cheek. Z suffers from a rare, unknown cerebral aneurysm and dies instantly from the minor slap. A had no knowledge that a slap was likely to cause death; s. 53 does not make A liable for murder.
distinctions: Different Act (s. 51) vs Different Effect (s. 53): Section 51 is about a distinct second act; Section 53 is about an unexpected graver consequence of the exact act abetted.
Knowledge of likelihood vs Actual intent: Under s. 53, constructive intent is imputed from the abettor's knowledge of likelihood.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an abettor who supplied kerosene to an accomplice instructing him to burn a rival's car is liable for culpable homicide when the car exploded and killed a nearby night watchman.
Rule: BNS s. 53 holds the abettor liable for a different effect if he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.
Application: Igniting a fuel tank in an occupied alley carries obvious known likelihood of explosion and mortal danger to nearby persons.
Conclusion: The abettor is liable for the death under s. 53.
